title: How Much Rent Can I Afford? Use Take-Home Pay
description: How much rent can I afford? Why the 30% rule misleads beginners, how to set a ceiling from take-home pay, and two worked examples.

cover.alt: A small model house sitting on top of a calculator

keywords: how much rent can i afford 30 percent rule rent calculator rent to income ratio take home pay
takeaways: The 30% rule uses gross pay, but you pay rent from take-home pay.
Use the lower of two ceilings: 30% of take-home pay, or what is left after your other costs.
Count utilities and travel, not just the rent.
body:
Search how much rent you can afford and almost every answer starts the same way: spend no more than 30% of your gross income. It sounds tidy. There is one problem. Gross income is your pay before tax and everything else comes out of it. It is not the money you live on, and nobody pays rent with the part of the paycheck that went to tax. So this guide does it the other way round. You will work from your take-home pay, the amount that lands in your bank account, and run two quick checks before you fall for a listing. There are worked examples for a part-time worker, a first salary, and two roommates who earn different amounts. And if nothing in your city fits any rule at all, there is a section on that too, because for plenty of people that is the real situation. ## Where the 30% rule comes from, and why it misleads beginners The 30% rule was never written as personal advice. It comes from the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), which counts a household as cost-burdened when housing takes more than 30% of its income, and severely cost-burdened above 50%. It has older roots in public housing policy: the Brooke Amendment of 1969 capped public housing rent at 25% of income, and changes in the early 1980s raised it to 30%. Governments use it to measure whole populations, a different job from telling one person what rent they can manage. Plenty of renters sit above the line. The US Census Bureau reported that in 2023, 49.7% of renter households, more than 21 million of them, spent over 30% of their income on housing. If your numbers come out above 30%, you are in the same position as about half the country. The real trap for a beginner is the word gross. On a first or low income, tax and other deductions take a solid bite out of the paycheck. Rent that looks fine at 30% of gross pay can quietly be 38% or 40% of the money that reaches your account. The lease still has to be paid from the smaller number, every month, including months when your hours drop. ## The take-home method, step by step ### Step 1: Find your real monthly take-home pay Look at your last two or three payslips, or the deposits in your bank account, and find the amount that actually arrived. Paid every two weeks? Multiply one paycheck by 26 and divide by 12 to get a monthly figure. If your pay jumps around, use a slow, normal month rather than your best one, because rent is due in the slow months too. If the lines on your payslip are a mystery, this walkthrough helps: [How to Read Your Paycheck](/blog/how-to-read-your-paycheck/). ### Step 2: Work out Ceiling A, the share check Take 30% of your take-home pay. That is the most that rent and utilities together should take in a month. Note the wording: rent and utilities, not rent alone. A cheap rent with heavy bills on top is not cheap housing. ### Step 3: Work out Ceiling B, the leftover check Write down what you already spend each month on everything except housing: food, transport, phone, toiletries, debt minimum payments, and a small amount for savings, even if it is only $40. Subtract that total from your take-home pay. What is left is the most housing could possibly take. This check matters because percentages ignore your actual bills: two people on the same pay have very different room for rent once a loan is in the picture. ### Step 4: Use the lower number Your rent ceiling is whichever check gives the smaller figure. Then shop a little under it. Listings leave things out, bills creep up, and a ceiling you can only meet in a perfect month is not a ceiling at all. If you would rather tap the numbers into a sheet than scribble them on paper, there is a free worksheet that walks through both ceilings for you.

Download the free Rent Affordability Worksheet (.xlsx)

It works in Google Sheets and Excel. No sign-up needed. ![The rent affordability worksheet showing two housing ceilings, a rent target and a check of one apartment](/assets/img/posts/rent-affordability-worksheet-preview-1080x619.webp) ## Worked example 1: a part-time worker The numbers here are made up to show the method. Say you work about 24 hours a week at $15 an hour: roughly $1,560 a month before tax, with $1,350 landing in your account. - The 30% rule on gross pay says rent of up to $468 sounds fine. - Ceiling A: 30% of $1,350 take-home is $405, for rent and utilities together. - Ceiling B: your other spending is $550 a month (food, transport, phone, small extras, $40 of savings), leaving $800. Ceiling A bites, so your ceiling is $405 all in. Here is why the difference matters. Rent at the gross-rule figure of $468, plus a $70 share of utilities, costs $538 a month, about 40% of your take-home pay. It works in a good month and hurts when your shifts get cut. At this income, the honest answer is usually a room in a shared house rather than a place of your own, and the price to compare is always the all-in price, not the headline rent. ## Worked example 2: a first salary of $38,000 Again, an illustration with made-up take-home figures. Say your first full-time job pays $38,000 a year: $3,167 a month before tax, and the 30% rule points you at rent of $950. Now run it on take-home pay. Say $2,600 a month reaches your account after tax and deductions. Ceiling A is 30% of that: $780 for rent and utilities combined. For Ceiling B, say your other monthly costs are $985: $320 on groceries, $180 on transport, $55 on your phone, a $160 student loan payment, $120 on going out and subscriptions, and $150 into savings. That leaves $1,615, so Ceiling A is the limit again. If utilities run about $130, your rent target is around $650. Follow the gross rule instead and the month looks like this: $950 of rent plus $130 of utilities is $1,080, about 41.5% of your take-home pay, and $300 a month more than the take-home method allows. That is $3,600 over a year, usually taken from the same pot that was meant to be your savings or your breathing room when something breaks. ## The same paycheck, two very different answers | Example (illustration) | Monthly gross pay | 30% rule, on gross | Monthly take-home pay | Ceiling A: 30% of take-home, rent + utilities | |----------------------------|-------------------|--------------------|-----------------------|-----------------------------------------------| | Part-time worker | $1,560 | $468 | $1,350 | $405 | | First job, $38,000 salary | $3,167 | $950 | $2,600 | $780 | Same jobs, same month. Only the starting figure changed, and the rent it points to drops by hundreds of dollars. ## Splitting rent when you and your roommate earn different amounts A 50/50 split sounds like the fair option, and it often is not. One more illustration. Say a two-bedroom place costs $1,650 a month. One roommate takes home $2,900 a month, the other $1,900. Split evenly, each pays $825: about 28% of the first roommate's pay, but about 43% of the second's. One of them is comfortable and the other is one bad week away from struggling, in the same flat. Splitting by income fixes that. Add the two take-home pays together: $4,800. The higher earner brings in about 60% of it, the lower earner about 40%. Apply the same split to the rent: the higher earner pays $997, the lower earner $653, and now each pays about 34% of their own pay. Split utilities the same way: on a $150 bill, about $91 and $59. The place costs the same. It just stops being easy for one person and heavy for the other. Agree the split before you view places, and get it in writing, even if it is just a message you both confirm. This guide covers the rest of the shared-bills conversation: [How to Split Bills With Roommates Fairly](/blog/how-to-split-bills-with-roommates/). ## When nothing in your city fits the rule You run the numbers, you search, and the cheapest decent place still eats 40% or more of your take-home pay. That is not a personal failure. When about half of renter households spend over 30% of their income on housing, the market is the problem as often as the budget is. ### Trim these first - Subscriptions and apps you barely open. Cancel them before signing a lease that leaves no slack. - Food delivery and takeaway food. Cooking most of the week is the biggest cut most people can make. - Your phone and internet plans. Cheaper tiers free up real money every month. - The shape of the home itself. A room in a shared house, a smaller place, or one neighbourhood over usually beats trimming small treats forever. - The rent itself. Asking for a lower rent in exchange for a longer lease sometimes works, and it costs nothing to ask: [How to Negotiate Rent](/blog/negotiate-your-rent/). ### What share is survivable for a year There is a difference between a stretch and a trap. Paying around 40% of take-home pay on housing can work for one fixed stretch, like a single 12-month lease, if your other costs are low, you have no large debt payments, you still save something small each month, and there is an end in sight, such as a pay rise or a planned move. Treat 40% as a bridge you cross, not a place you live. Past about half your take-home pay, the maths stops forgiving: one cut in hours or one broken phone and the rent itself is at risk. ### The longer commute that costs more than it saves The standard fix for high rent is moving further out. Sometimes it works. Sometimes the cheaper place costs more once you count the travel. Run both totals, like this illustration. A place near work costs $1,250 a month plus a $60 travel pass: $1,310 all in. A place further out costs $1,050, which looks like a $200 saving. But now you drive: about 30 extra miles a day, 22 work days a month, is 660 extra miles. At 30 miles per gallon that is 22 gallons of fuel, about $77, plus $120 a month for parking. Driving costs $197 against the $60 pass, so the real saving shrinks to about $63 a month, in exchange for roughly 33 extra hours a month on the road: under $2 an hour for your own time. Add tolls or a second bus and the far place can cost more than the near one. ## The landlord's math is not your math One last number you will meet while applying: many landlords ask for gross income of at least three times the monthly rent. On a $1,500 rent, that means showing $4,500 a month before tax. That test answers the landlord's question, whether you look able to pay. It does not answer yours, which is whether paying leaves you enough to live on. Passing their check and affording the place are two different things, so run your own two ceilings either way. Keep the one-off costs of moving in separate from this decision, too. Deposits and basic furniture are a savings goal of their own, covered here: [First Apartment Costs](/blog/first-apartment-costs/). ## Frequently asked questions ### Should I work out rent from my gross pay or my take-home pay? Use take-home pay for your own decision, because that is the money you actually have. Gross pay only matters because landlords and the old 30% rule use it. If the two figures point to different rents, trust the take-home one. ### What if the cheapest place I can find is 40% of my take-home pay? It can work for a fixed period, like one lease, if your other spending is low, you still save a small amount monthly, and there is an end in sight. It stops working when it becomes permanent, or pushes past half your pay. Treat the lease length as your deadline to change the situation. ### Should utilities count inside the percentage? Yes. Judge the total cost of living in the place: rent, utilities, parking, and any regular fees the lease adds. Two places with the same rent can differ by $150 a month once bills are counted. ### My pay changes from month to month. Which month should I use? Use a slow, typical month, not your best one, and not an average that includes a rare bumper month. Rent is the same in your worst month as in your best. This guide goes deeper on planning around uneven pay: [How to Budget With Irregular Income](/blog/budget-with-irregular-income/). ### What if I have debt payments as well? Then the leftover check matters more than the percentage. Rent that leaves no room for your minimum payments costs you twice, once in the payment and again in interest and fees. If the two checks disagree, take the lower figure and treat any extra as debt money, not rent money. This article is general information, not personal financial advice. Rent rules, taxes, and tenancy law differ between countries and areas, so check the rules where you live and run your own numbers before signing a lease. ## Sources - [U.S. Census Bureau, Nearly Half of Renter Households Are Cost-Burdened, Proportions Differ by Race (September 12, 2024), reporting 2023 American Community Survey data](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024/renter-households-cost-burdened-race.html) - [Apartment List, How Much Rent Can I Afford?
